answerNotes.RICE: Rice is a grain that absorbs water as it cooks. The word names the grain, not the pot or the cooking method.
answerNotes.LID: A lid is a removable cover. On a cooking pot it helps contain heat and steam; on a jar it closes the opening.
answerNotes.GRAIN: Grain can mean an edible seed or the pattern of wood fibers. The food and woodworking scenes use different senses of the same word.
answerNotes.POT: Pot can name a cooking vessel or a plant container. The surrounding clues tell you which everyday use is intended.
answerNotes.WATER: Water is the same liquid whether it is in a drinking glass, a garden hose, or a cooking pot. The container changes the scene, not the substance.
answerNotes.FORK: A fork's prongs hold pieces of food. A garden fork is a larger tool sharing that pronged shape.
answerNotes.WHITE: White is a color description, not a flower or bird name. Crossings can help when a clue asks for a color rather than a species.
answerNotes.CUP: Cup can name a drinking vessel or a measuring amount. A recipe's measured cup is not simply any small mug.

answerNotes.LEMON: Lemon juice is sour. Zest is the thin colored outer peel used for flavor, not the thick white layer beneath it.
answerNotes.FISH: Fish live in water and breathe through gills. A seal or otter swims too, but it is a mammal rather than a fish.

answerNotes.WEDGE: A wedge narrows toward one edge or point. A lemon wedge and a cheese wedge share that shape but are different foods.
answerNotes.JUICE: Juice is liquid released from fruit or vegetables. Pulp is the soft plant material that may remain mixed into it.
answerNotes.PAN: Pan is a broad kitchen word. A frying pan is used on a stove, while a loaf pan holds dough or batter in the oven.
answerNotes.BAKE: Baking uses dry heat in an oven. Boiling instead cooks food in bubbling liquid.
